utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we continue, could I mention one matter. There was a motion for certification from a decision of the Chamber to allow an appeal on an order about approaching of witnesses. Because of the urgency of the matter in the trial, the Chamber gave its decision, it was filed, and then we find the next day that a response from the Defence was filed. I would simply note on the record that the main thrust of the response was an argument of the Prosecution on which the Chamber did not rely in its decision. And there were other matters which were all essentially a repeat of what was said in the first submission. There is no change in the Chamber's attitude from the response. So the decision stands and will not be modified. Good morning, sir. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we started to speak about the position of town commander, a local commander. And I have just a few questions on that. The organisation of a detention facility, that's not a typical or usual duty for an anti-aircraft defence commander, is that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's because anti-aircraft defence commanders are not generally concerned with the administration of a prison camp.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unless as a special role for inter play within his own deployment sector and unless a special mission was assigned to him in addition to being the chief of PVO. But if he has other roles to play in the area, then it can be one of his commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it make sense to appoint an anti-aircraft commander to oversee a prison camp, or are there other persons, such as military police or security organ, who would be in a better position and better trained to do this sort of role?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly be expected to go into any decisions that the commander of the 80th brigade made at the time. It's his right to make these calls. It's a matter of his own assessment. Yesterday we talked about the duties of the commander of the artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir the question is: Whether or not -- you're an experienced officer -- whether or not it makes sense to appoint an anti-aircraft defence officer or commander to administer a prison camp, or is that a better role -- or is that a role for the security organ or military police who are trained to do that type of job? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Let me tell you this, first. The commander or the chief of security, no [Realtime transcript read in error "in a"] way; they must cover all the units. In that case, that means that he could not possibly be, because that would be a renouncing on his basic fundamental tasks and assignments. That's one thing. Secondly, the military police was low, in terms of manpower. So for someone to be a local commander, this person would need to have experience. They would need to know what to do. They would need to enjoy some authority. This was an active duty officer, the commander of an artillery battalion, and then the commander would probably judge that a professional would be perfectly able to do this, to perform this task. Someone who was a professional. And all the other men there were reservists and that's my opinion. If I'd been commander of the 80th Brigade I would probably have made the same decision, especially in view of the fact that there had been a previous order regulating that his command post should be right there. The commander of the 80th Brigade only wanted to do the best possible thing, and he appointed those people in the belief that they could perform their duty and that they could ensure impeccable order in their own area of responsibility or rather in the area covered by their command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small correction, page 3, line 2. The witness said: Chief of security, no way. That was precisely what the witness said, but that was not reflected on the transcript. So the meaning is lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like me to clarify it with the witness or can we just take the translation, that's what I thought I heard, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is no debate over an, an interjection over a translation, or interpretation, I should say, we simply leave the matter on the basis that the mistake is corrected by the transcript. If there's a dispute about the matter, I'm sure we would hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever received training in prison camp administration?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a unit commander, I had to. That was part of our military training at the academy, too. We tackled certain subjects in relation to that type of business. I'm talking about security in general; such topics were studied. In the army we had general training and specialised training, every month. There were two seven-hour terms. We tackled some practical and theoretical subjects. As for this particular area, the chief of security, Colonel Sljivancanin, carried this out in relation to the officers of the Guards Brigade. Let alone what had been done before the Guards Brigade had even arrived, this is a commitment, this is a duty. Otherwise how else would you take steps? If no training has been performed already, how do you know what to do? There had to be training at all levels before anything at all was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially just before this assignment was received, that the guards eventually received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said you had training in security. Did you have training, did you receive training in being a prison camp administrator which is specialized training, did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Among other things, treatment of prisoners is part of -- well, this is preceded by training, what to do at what time. We did that. The artillery battalion commander of the 80th did that, he's a professional soldier. From the level of the security administration, we even had some topics that were imposed on us and that had to be dealt with within the year. And I remember exactly that there were such topics, there were practical diagrams showing how this was to be dealt with. Receiving prisoners, bringing them in, securing prisoners, the procedure separating them, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when did you receive this training, sir? When did you particularly receive this training?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this training was, I can't say when, which month, but that was part of the annual training plan. But it gained in importance considerably, just before the assignment was received, meaning when the command of the Guards Brigade got this assignment, that one in relation to Vukovar, among other things, that topic and all the other topics were dealt with, with all the officers in the Guards Brigade and I assume that this was also done with all the others who were supposed to be involved or who were envisaged to be involved on this or similar assignments, because this was the sort of thing one came across, this was the sort of thing that was expected in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we of the Guards Brigade had an interim plan --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just finish, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade was not part of the Guards Brigade, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that the 80th Motorised Brigade had much more training than most other brigades, isn't that correct? The 80th Motorised Brigade had much more training than the -- than -- I'm sorry, than -- the Guards Motorised Brigade had much more training than the 80th Motorised Brigade, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree on that; all that's a matter of course. The Guards Brigade was an elite unit. 99 per cent of its manpower was made up of professional officers, all the more reason for the commander to make this decision, to assign a single professional officer to receive that particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir you haven't reviewed the records of the archives of the 80th Motorised Brigade to see what, if any, training those people had, have you?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't one of my duties. I do know, however, that Colonel Sljivancanin, when among other things the 80th Brigade became part of Operations Group South, or rather he stepped up training in relation to his own area. We knew that these were reservists and precisely to prevent any trouble, any misuse, any surprises due to an absence of proper training.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may? And I apologise to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It's the transcript on page 6, the witness's answer, lines 13 through 17, I think the witness said something else, and what the answer says makes no sense at all. It says 99 per cent of its manpower was made up of professional officers, and then it says that this commander was assigned because -- one of the few professionals in the brigade, if my colleague could please clarify that, because it appears to make no sense at all the way it stands. I'm sure there must be some sort of error.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript, it says: "99 per cent of the manpower was made up of professional officers," and you're referring to the Guards Brigade. Do you mean professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in reference to the Guards Brigade only and its professional soldiers, the professional soldiers of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now you just mentioned training by major Sljivancanin. Were you present with Major Sljivancanin at the 80th Motorised Brigade when he or any of his deputies gave any training to those persons? Were you present for that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present. Why should I have been? This is a specialised thing, I had my own commitments each of us had our own commitments that we in charge of. What business would we possibly have had checking on each other? No need for that. Secondly, we all knew each other quite well in the Guards Brigade. It would have been quite superfluous for anyone to go and check on what anybody else was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This, sir, wasn't the Guards Brigade. This was the 80th Motorised Brigade that we're talking about. So you don't know what, if any, training they were having, they were receiving and you weren't present for any training; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is totally immaterial. It doesn't matter if I was present or not. Please don't twist things around. When you said that Mr. Sljivancanin was carrying out training, was I present? I answered that one, didn't I? There is no need to check on Major Sljivancanin. He knew how to do his job. He did his job. It would have been quite superfluous for me, as someone as a chief of a branch to go and check on him. That was not the established practice in the Guards Brigade. We were all sufficiently trained to know what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you were in the Guards Brigade for three years, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during that time, you served with major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you served with Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you served with Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the esteemed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known Colonel Mrksic for a long time. He have met him several years before I came to the Guards Brigade. He had been my commander in the Guards Brigade for three years. And for four years, or rather I might not quite be dead on, for about four years in the special unit corps. Since after 1992 when the special unit corps was set up, I left the Guards Brigade and joined this new unit that had Colonel Mrksic at its head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately the same amount of time. Before arriving in the Guards Brigade. We weren't particularly close, but I knew him and we worked together later on. For the following five or six years. I know him quite well. All three of them, in fact. And they know me too, it goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're very proud having served in the Guards Brigade, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, I am proud of the job that I did throughout my career and especially my time with the Guards Brigade and with the special unit corps. If you allow, I would just like to say a couple of words. The name itself, the Guards Brigade, there is just one unit like that in the army. There was at the time, just one unit like that, so it's nature is quite peculiar. If I tell you that my joining the Guards Brigade and my last departure when I went to work with the Defence ministry, it was the longest possible procedure, regardless of the fact that all the other preconditions were in place, training, good marks, but selection is what it is, that people were selected. First class soldiers, officers. In addition, or despite the fact that some officers met the criteria for some other units, that doesn't mean they were up to scratch for the Guards Brigade. There were special selection criteria for the Guards Brigade because it was an elite unit in every possible way. It set an example for all the other units in the army to follow in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you wouldn't want to see anything besmirch its reputation, would you?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. God forbid. And there is nothing that could possibly besmirch his reputation. I think the Guards Brigade carried out the assignment that it received and you have to know that this was no combat unit, so that's an aggravating circumstance, if anything. This was a protocol unit, a security unit, a parade unit. So it received an assignment, it successfully carried out preparations, it made an assessment, it made a decision, and it carried out this mission to the extent that it was able to. In an honourable honest, and top-quality way. As any other units, it carried out its tasks in its own area, in its own country, in its own state for the benefit and for the sake of its own people, thereby preventing anything from happening that might have disrupted or endangered its integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been no interventions, well probably then -- can I please conclude? It's not very good for you to interrupt me halfway through my answer. If you don't want me to answer, please say so straight away, after all it's you asking all of these questions. So if you want to keep on asking these questions please allow me to answer them. As any proper country, this country had to do something to make sure there was order within its borders. Terrorists, sabotage, and other such units renegade units that attacked the people of Yugoslavia, something had to be done to restore order. You had to do something about it just like any other well organised country. It is a well-known fact how terrorists are dealt with. By force. Or else we're not really fulfilling our mission, are we? We simply did not have the privilege of being given a chance not to carry out our mission. Our constitutional commitment was to make sure there was order and to protect our constitution, and this constitution had been placed in great danger, and had been jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said this constitution had been placed in great danger and had been jeopardised. Was that by the Ustasha who you referred to yesterday and you referred to in your documents?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two categories, the constitution is the highest legal act of a country, defining and specifying the organisational structure and everything else, and as for Ustashas, what else could they be but terrorists? This is a gang, a renegade gang, which, thanks to those forces, extreme forces, which were against the system as it existed at the time, embarked upon an armed conflict against their own people. Not just the Serbs, but against their own people, the Croats who did not support them. So what else was the army supposed to do? To allow the paramilitary to organise life or to prevent it? Who else was in charge? Who else under the constitution had the responsibility to deal with this? This is precisely why armies exist. Nowadays we have a lot of similar examples as to how to combat terrorism. Every country has to do it, otherwise it will disappear. Politics is another matter, and politicians fail to reach an agreement. They fail to reach a political, proper political settlement, to involve the army. The army was duty bound to carry out this task. Back at the time, and also in 1999, I was proud of the mission I carried out in this country for my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that your unit was well trained and disciplined the guards motorised brigade. The other units in Vukovar, would you agree the reserve units, the TOs, the Seselj-supported unit, those were not as disciplined or well trained. Don't you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are two categories. When it comes to training and discipline, you know the saying, there is chaff in all kinds of wheat. So this is why there is a system in place. This is why it is placed under control, precisely so that such occurrences can be prevented. As for training --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir? Sir --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and capabilities, well I wouldn't say that they were incompetent, but definitely there was a different level of capabilities. What professional army does is one thing. And it's quite a different matter how long a reserve unit needs in order to be brought up to the same level. So naturally, there is a significant difference in the level of their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one hand you have professional soldiers and on the other hand you have reserve forces, consisting of people who, until recently, did very different types of jobs. They were civilians. , and then you needed this training to be conducted very quickly to bring them up to speed, you know, and we had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- organise all kinds of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Leva Supoderica unit which was sponsored by the Serbian Radical Party, Seselj's party, do you know what level of training those volunteers had?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you about the level of training. I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, no, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They weren't trained, okay. Now you said you carried what you referred to as an aide memoire.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, yesterday you testified that you carried an aide memoire relating to the Geneva conventions.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I have it with me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that other members of the Guards Motorised Brigade also carried them, too?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you realise that carrying one of those by itself or the fact that you carry one by itself is not sufficient to prevent a war crime from occurring. Would you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't carry it just for the sake of carrying a piece of paper with us. This was supposed to serve as a reminder for all of us as right reminder of what we learned during our training and that was something that went to show how much attention the commander of the brigade paid to this matter, precisely in order to prevent any possible abuse --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and lack of discipline and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The fact that you carried that document by itself, would you agree is not sufficient to prevent a war crime?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you, you are focusing just on this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there was something that preceded the paper; there were preparations and training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I must interfere. We've sat here with patience for some time. You are talking at very great length, sir, not about the question that is put to you. Will you please listen to the question, and answer it. Or we will be here all day and into next week while you give very expansive views about matters you are not asked about. So please pay attention to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The fact that you carried that sheet of paper by itself is not sufficient to prevent war crimes, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paper has nothing to do with it. It can be of assistance, and then again it doesn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that a member of the Guards Brigade has come to this court and has admitted to having committed murders at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that there has been testimony in this court that members of the Guards Motorised Brigade or officers were present when crimes were committed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether members of the Vukovar TO, whether the volunteers or the Seselj unit members from the Leva Supoderica unit carried aide memoires in relation to the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say. I didn't go and check that, but I know that General Mrksic in a meeting ordered that whatever we had within the Guards Brigade ought to be copied and distributed to other units which became part of OG South, from the moment the guards took over that function. Now, whether it was indeed distributed to all of the troops who were out in the field, I really don't know but commands at various levels received this, I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well sir do you know what if any training the members of Seselj's Leva Supoderica unit had in relation to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of Seselj's visit to Vukovar in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember he came once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of his statement to troops: Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As an experienced officer and a commander, you realise the danger in saying that to volunteers, TO members, or persons who want revenge. There is a serious danger there, isn't there, sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There can be serious danger, but we didn't come there for ceremonial purposes. There was a conflict underway at, a combat against renegade groups that were prepared to do anything. So what were we supposed to do? To wait for them to liquidate us so that we would not return to Belgrade? These were gangs of outlaws, either they had to be liquidated or they had to surrender. What else were we supposed to do? Beg them to surrender? What else does one do with terrorists? Either you liquidate them, or they liquidate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified that the Guards Motorised Brigade took command of the OG South, and you used the date of November 8th, and that the next day, on November 9th, you drafted that anti-aircraft defence task document. Do you recall that testimony? And that's on pages 12146 and 12147.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct that. I really have trouble remembering all of the dates now. Whether it was on the 8th or perhaps a few days earlier. I can't remember that now. But it's not relevant at any rate. What is relevant is that on the 9th, when the commander adopted a decision, decision as to what needed to be done with the PVO, all other commanders, in turn, proceeded with their plans, as part of that original operations order of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that General Mrksic took command of the Operational Group South a full month earlier, on October 8th, 1991. Not on November 8th?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't hold me to it. I really wouldn't be able to say the exact date right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that throughout -- from October 8th on, General Mrksic was in command of the Operation Group South and was issuing orders during that time, to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that commander General Mrksic issued orders when he was there, except when he was away on business. Be it that he reported to the commander of the military district, or perhaps defence secretary, and such situations are well regulated in the army; if he was absent, his deputy would step in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 401, please. Page 17 in the English and also 17 in the B/C/S, which is 02935450 is the specific page in the B/C/S. It relates to the war diary October 8th at 0810 hours or 8.10 in the morning. Do you see that? There are five points?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it says "OG duty takeover" in the first, and it also --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Says Colonel [indiscernible] Thanked everyone for their cooperation and wished them success in the future. That's October 8th. Do you recall Colonel Mrksic taking control of the Operational Group South on that date? Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So Colonel Mrksic did not take control on November 18th, and you -- I'm sorry on November 8th, and then you, then, prepared and filed those anti-aircraft tasks on the following day.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, we misunderstood each other. On the 9th, on the 9th of November, an assignment was issued and we did what we did. There was an order and a plan. And this other date is the date when the commander took over responsibilities of the commander of OG South, the commander of the Guards Brigade did. That wasn't on the 8th of November. Maybe it was a slip of tongue on my part, when I mentioned the dates earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another issue, sir. Yesterday you testified as to how long Operations Group South lasted and you referred to Exhibit 425. And you said that there was a handover of files on the 22nd of November, that the files and archives were handed over to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said documents for command and control, but not the archives. The archives remain with the unit. They cannot be moved. Everybody ensures that their archives remain with them. Archives and records. But as for command and control documents, then, yes. They were turned over to the command of the 80th Brigade, and that brigade from that moment on took over the role of the command in that area. And as for the Guards Brigade, they prepared for their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well maybe it was another slip of the tongue, because in your testimony on page 12142, you said: "The entire command archive, all the files, the so-called secret command TKT was handed over to the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac." So are you now saying the archives were not handed over?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the archives. Command and control documents, yes. How can the command turn over to somebody else their archives and remain without them? It is not done. The command and control documents are turned over, so that the command, which remains on a location, can communicate with the superior command on whose strength it is and pursuant to whose order it took over that role, and that was the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that Operation Group South continued to function on November 22nd, on November 23rd; that it did not cease to function on November 22nd?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It functioned for one more day, because there was some structures within its composition and it had to ensure that they returned to their original units. And so that it returned all supplies that it received, ordnance, other supplies, food, and things like that. And in order to do that, they had to function as the operations group, because they had initially taken that over. But they were no longer in the role of the command, in that area. And there was no way that they could continue in that role, because they had nothing more to do with the 1st Military District, because pursuant to an order of the command of the 1st Military District, that role was turned over to the 80th Brigade and it was that Brigade that resolved all issues in that area. We were dealing with these other issues. We had to turn over the supplies that we had received initially, and we had to prepare for our return to Belgrade. And that was on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 426, please. In the B/C/S it is only one page, it is 04638417. Do you see that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's a document from the commander of Operations Group South, commander -- Colonel Mile Mrksic, to the 1st Military District? And that's the daily combat report that was sent at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it discusses various matters of their involvement during the day, ranging from orders to combat activities, if any, and who they met.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that is correct. I have to add that the 80th Brigade had very basic supplies and equipment. They were not really equipped to do this properly and to send it to the command of the 1st Military District. I know this because I was present when it was agreed to send this particular report, because, as far as I can remember, on the very next day, the commander of the 80th Brigade wrote reports in his own hand, because he didn't have the equipment needed in order to type it. That was the situation with them. And that was on that day alone. Because we had to discharge our regular duty to the 1st Military District in a proper way, but we no longer had any command authority. As soon as you turn over command authorities, all your rights that existed until that moment, ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree with me at the bottom of that letter Colonel Mrksic signs it as OG South commander, and he was still the commander of the Operations Group South on November 23rd, 1991, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did sign this, and he turned the documents over. As I told you, he continued in the role for as long as he needed to deal with all of the equipment, material and equipment that we had initially received. And he had to return all of that, because this was not received in the name of the guards Brigade but rather in the name of OG South and that had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you will notice number 3: Two delegations visited OG South area of responsibility, AOR, today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is not contentious. Out there, in the field, it is impossible to just take the scissors and cut off all existing obligations. OG South exists no longer, let us just get into our cars and go back home. We couldn't do that. We had spent there a long period of time, in combat. So I don't quite understand whether you have a proper idea of just what a task it is in order to close it down within 14 hours. It's not just a matter of cutting a ribbon, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But it says at the top, on the left: OG South command. It doesn't say: Former OG South command. It doesn't say ex OG South command. It says OG South command. Doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not typical in the military terminology to use former. Why would they say "former"? I don't see anything questionable about this, because the commitments or the duties were turned over on the previous day. And OG South was duty bound to report on that in their following daily report too, and to cover the period of time from the previous report. We don't need to go into details now to ensure that that's what it is. Most likely it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at number 1: There were no Ustasha activities in the OG South area of responsibility today.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So OG South still had an area of responsibility as of that day, according to this document from the commander of OG South to the 1st Military District, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been nothing contentious, even if the commander had written that. But he could not have written that. How can he write a report about a 24 hour period? How can the commander of the 80th Brigade write that? He was not the commander of OG South. He was just the local commander. Operations Group South did not continue after the 22nd. So the commander of the 80th Brigade was not the commander of OG South. How can he write in the report for the previous day? From the previous report, so there is 24 hours. And in the meantime there had been a change, and Operations Group South ceased to function as an institution, or as a command. Someone had to write this, and as I said, as I said at the outset, the 80th Brigade had exceptionally modest equipment. It couldn't have. The commander wrote his reports by hand. He didn't type them because he had nothing to type them with, and then he would send them to the command at the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir this document does not say: Area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade, does it?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This document does not --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This document does not say that the 80th Motorised Brigade is now in command of Vukovar. It doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a document, I can't tell you off-the-cuff where it is. I don't have it on me, but there is a document regulating tasks and obligations, and with a deadline set for the takeover by the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you want to leave it that this document was filed by Colonel Mrksic as the commander of Operation Group South, even though Operations Group South ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is beyond dispute. This is a document that was sent. There is no doubt about that. It was signed by the commander. There is no dilemma. But he was no longer in command of the forces Operations Group South was beginning to dissolve. If you look at the last title on the last passage it says, "to the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade was given every organisational and specialised assistance to deal with all the questions, in terms of taking responsibility in the area of responsibility of OG South." What more do you need to submit to a superior command?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But it doesn't say that they have taken over responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there must be a document somewhere stating precisely when the documents were taken over. The takeover of command and control documents, when that happens the commander of OG South has no further possibility to exercise command, simply because he doesn't have the necessary documents. He's no longer connected to the operation centre of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But as we said yesterday we're not going to speculate, sir. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning to all. I would like to pick up where my learned friend has just left off and could we please have Exhibit 426 on our monitors again. Thank you very much. Mr. Lesanovic, this is a regular combat report, isn't it? In relation to which period?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24 hours before, everything that happened between 1800 hours, well it starts at 1700 hours and then goes on until 1800 hours on the 22nd [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So do we have the developments on the 22nd of November, 1991 reflected in this report?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. As I said, everything that started happening after 1800 hours and didn't make it into the previous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we please now scroll down a little and look at the lower half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there appears to be an error in the transcript, page 24, line 22, it says it starts -- it's a 24 hour -- 24 hours before everything that happened, between 1800 hours, well it's it says 1700 hours and goes on to 1800 hours on the 22nd, I think it should be the 23rd. The 24-hour period from the 22nd to the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. If you are unhappy with that, Mr. Vasic, you can take it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, and I will clarify this point with the witness, Your Honours. I think that the situation was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, this report that you see in front of you, which period of time is that in relation to? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a regular combat report, the same one that I spoke about yesterday. More specifically in relation to this, it's about the period between 1700 hours, 2000 hours, 22nd of November. Until 1700 hours on the 23rd of November. So in relation to a 24-hour period. Secondly, this is in relation to this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is between 1700 hours on the 22nd of November until 1700 hours on the 23rd of November. What this means is, on the 22nd the command of Operations Group South was still in existence and functioning. I believe this report is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add something. Why does it say 18? Let's clarify this. This is the period when all the incoming reports must be processed and prepared for delivery. That's why it says 18. And that's what the superior said should be done. They are sent at 18 with the situation as before. It's a cross-section of time. And then you have 17 hours and then this flows over into the next report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your opinion. Please pay attention to the portion of this report that begins with "the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade". And please read, again, this part of the report, but slowly. And please specify the time when this part of the report was produced.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of the 80th Motorised Brigade was given every professional organisational and material support to deal with all issues related to taking over responsibility in the area of responsibility of OG South." That's the activity. This went on the previous day. It lasted for as long as it lasted. It's probably written down somewhere. There is -- professional bodies went there. Given the fact that this had been going on the previous day, it had to make it into this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me about the phrasing in this document. Is this in the past tense in the B/C/S? This activity has at this point been completed, right?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely it. It doesn't say support is being given or provided. It says: Support was provided. So this is something that was carried out as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You talked about TKT documents yesterday. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secret command of troops tables, signals, maps, coded maps, signals, equipment, operative instructions, aide memoires for those on duty, books where observations are recorded. Because he has to open his book the moment he receives a new assignment and a new role. And from that moment on, he is on the line to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were asked by my learned friend about the level of training of the units and members of the JNA, the rules used to organise, establish and control detention. Mr. Lesanovic, what about these schools that JNA officers go to? Is this sort of thing a subject that was taught at those schools, detention-related issues?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. There were certain subjects and topics that were part of the curriculum. Regardless of the branch or service. Everyone received some training in that area. We're soldiers and we could end up in all sorts of situations in our military career, regardless of the branch of service. Everybody had a range of subjects that they were supposed to go through, let alone one's active service. That was a commitment. There were annual plans to train officers and NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to these wartime subjects, so to speak, what about detention issues in the JNA? Isn't this something that service in the garrison, in the garrison and barracks also entailed?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the rules governing detention of prisoners were also rules that were applied in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were applied wherever there were detention units. Not all the barracks had a detention unit, but that did not absolve any officers from their responsibility to deal with this because one simply never knew when, in the course of one's career, one might find oneself in a situation when an assignment was received and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This sort of training, what you've spoken about now, the sort of training received by JNA officers, was the same sort of training provided for reserve officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly. During their training, during their education, during their time with their unit and especially after being assigned to a war unit within their own commands. There were regular plans for calling up the reservists for training. So it was as part of the training that military and specialised training was carried out as well as subjects from the same area, security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My learned friend asked you about local commanders and the powers that they exercised in places where they were appointed. What about these commanders, did they have the obligation to follow the rules of service, the same ones that applied to the garrisons and barracks, including organising detention?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The only questions I asked about town commanders was yesterday concerning a -- a prior inconsistent statement and today concerning the issue of administration of prison facilities. There was no questioning beyond that. There was nothing in relation to the rules and regulations of garrisons and other matters and barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. But the subject having been opened, I would not regard these questions as being outside what might properly follow from what you have asked. So carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You've heard the question. Please answer it.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything envisaged in the rules of service, everything that applied to the work and life in the barracks, when it came to detention, the same thing applied to local commanders. How else could they have dealt with this? There had to be a document. And this was the principal document. There is no dilemma about this. Everything is very well defined and clear as a spring day at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, yesterday you were answering a question by my learned friend and you were talking about the position on the 18th of November, 1991 taken by the command of the LAD PVO artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade. You were shown the war diary of the 80th Brigade and the war diary of the guards Brigade. And you were asked to comment on certain entries. First of all, let me ask you this. Do you know who took over the area of responsibility which at one time, during the operations in Vukovar, was held by the 20 Partisan Brigade which was part of the 46th partisan artillery battalion?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at one point within OG South there was the 20th Partisan Brigade and if so where exactly was it deployed, in what area?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th Partisan Brigade was deployed in the Ovcara area. Can you give me a hand with this please? Vucevo [phoen], wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's not speculate. Can we please have 156. It's a map, and you can use that to get your bearings, sir. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify the positions held by the 20th Partisan Brigade, if so, can the Usher please hand you the magic pen.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may not be perfectly accurate, but it's about Ovcara and the surrounding area. Perhaps even further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please use a number 1 to mark that.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably a broader area than the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you circle the broader area, then. Put a number 2 there please. Thank you. Can you please tell me after the withdrawal of the 20th partisan Brigade, who took over this area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I move that this drawing be admitted into evidence, and we shall no longer be requiring it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's exhibit 774, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit 401. The B/C/S is 02935478. And the English is 35, page 35. While we're waiting, this is an entry in the war diary of the Guards Brigade and the date is the 18th of November, 1991. My learned friend talked to you about this entry yesterday. Page 02935478. Thank you. The lower half of the page, please. My learned friend showed you this entry yesterday, but as far as I realise, it wasn't read into its entirety yesterday. Can you please read the entire entry and tell me who was present at this meeting where this order was given.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean you want me to read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Silently, yes. Not out loud. And just tell us who the commander had summoned.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this war diary, you see that the commander of OG South summoned the commander of the 20th Partisan Brigade, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and the commander of the armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade as well as the division commander, the guards division commander in order to coordinate taction on pulling the 20th Partisan Brigade out of the combat disposition, and also in order to take responsibility for closing the axis crossing Ovcara and Jakobovac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would a meeting like this constitute a handover of an area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders followed from this, as defined by the commander, and these orders were carried out. When you have a handover, the area is taken over, one unit leaves the area. Another unit arrives. So that's it. All that follows is a report on a mission that has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who reports on assignments that were carried out, in an area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both commanders. The commander who is on his way out and the commander who is on his way in. Both. If there are any problems they are their dealt with immediately, but there shouldn't be any, because this is all dealt with prior to an assignment being received. And of course having received an assignment, knowing the commander, he would have allowed for questions, for questions to be asked if there was anything that still wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could orders issued directly to units or through the commands of those brigades taking over an area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see what is done in the army, the top people, the commanders, those most responsible, those in charge of carrying it out. In order to have this implemented, they made their own proposals, among other things in this other thing you can see that, and I know that the commander of the 80th proposed for this to be shifted. He requested that, and that became part of the order, this order that he is supposed to carry out. And the move was then executed by the commander of the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about this entry, my learned friend asked you about the signature, Major Trifunovic. What does that mean? This signature in this war diary, what does it mean? We didn't clarify that yesterday, did we can you please return us to the top of the page? Can we please scroll up to the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, it says, signature of person entering information. This should be an operations officer, but it doesn't necessarily have to be. It's whoever is ordered to do it that enters this information. The war diary is a summary of what matters, what is essential, what happened in any one of the units, any activities that the units undertook, assignments in abbreviated form, reports; everything, in short. But the important thing is to have an overview of what happens over a certain period of time. Time as in terms of time or during a day. It depends on the dynamics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please. You're talking about the war diary. You were looking at the operations war log yesterday, too. Which information is more complete under the military rules, those in the war diary or those in the operations war log?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operations log should be kept in peacetime. A war diary is a wartime document. The usual thing, though, once these activities have been completed, then this war diary is filed away, along with all the other documents and then there is a certain period of time where you know nothing about what goes on. It is for this reason that both these documents are kept, and produced, but it is the war diary, as I said yesterday, that remains for the future. Of course, mistakes are always possible. Errors in terms of dates, in terms of erroneous information being recorded and so on and so forth. It is human to err.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a good time for our break and I'm very near the end of my redirect, therefore I will not be needing much more time after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will resume at five minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, let us continue with our redirect. Yesterday, my learned friend showed Exhibit 375 to you, which is the war log book of the 80th Brigade. Could we see this on our screens, please, this exhibit. Thank you. Could you please zoom in this portion with the text, please. This is fine. Thank you. My colleague asked you about some entries and the questions had to do with permanent or regular tasks, ongoing tasks. Can you explain that term? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a task that has a permanent quality, a task that is constant, that is constantly there, that doesn't need to be repeated, that constantly applies and we don't need to re-enter it. This was the assignment given by the command of the 80th Brigade. So this ongoing permanent task or assignment is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And from whom did he receive this permanent ongoing task?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the commander of OG South, when all tasks were defined for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me who is in charge of implementing this ongoing permanent task that the commander of OG South gave to the command of the 80th brigade and who reports to the commander of OG South about the implementation of the ongoing or permanent task and any progress therein. Just wait for the interpretation to complete, please.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only person responsible and relevant for this is the person who was given this task or assignment. That is to say, the commander of the 80th Brigade. He is the one who reports, in his daily reports, on the level of implementation of this task and any other problems that might arise. He sends in his requests in case he needs something and if there is something significantly affecting the implementation of his task, then he can send in an interim request without waiting for the daily report. But it is only the commander of the 80th Brigade that can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that all of these orders issued by the commander of OG South including permanent tasks and additional tasks, all of this is sent to the commander of units, in this case the commander of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, it is sent to the commanders of subordinate units who, in turn, send it further on. They assign tasks to various people, depending on the role, nature and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lesanovic. My learned friend cross-examined you today about your attitude towards the Guards Brigade, your attitude about preserving and protecting the reputation of this brigade. Let me ask you this: Would you conceal, from any court, including this one, anything you know in order to protect the reputation of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for that. No need to conceal anything, because in carrying out tasks and assignments, there was nothing secret. Regardless of the role and position of the brigade, I would have never put myself in a situation to lie, because there was nothing to lie about. There is no reason not to say the truth. The truth is present. There is no reason whatsoever to conceal anything. I didn't come here to tell you untruths. I came here to tell the truth; to assist the Chamber in resolving some matters and to assist other people because I think that this is an integral component of my duty to my unit, the unit in which I carried out many tasks and the unit in which I would do the same thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lesanovic for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is one matter perhaps, maybe more, that you may be able to assist the Chamber with, Mr. Lesanovic. On the 20th of November, 1991, did you have any connection with Ovcara that day?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, as I stated yesterday, and as it happened from the morning hours until 1500 hours, I was involved with investigative organs and General Stankovic, who is the current defence minister and a pathologist. We were exhuming and identifying three soldiers who had been burnt down by Ustashas. Following that, I went back to my post, which was in the sector of the winery observation post. I stayed there briefly in order to gather information, and to prepare myself for the briefing which was to be held at the headquarters of the commander of OG South at 1700 hours. On that day, in the meantime Colonel Caric had arrived. I exchanged a few sentences with him and then proceeded to the briefing. After the briefing, I stayed there for a short period of time. I had a coffee at the headquarters, at the command post. I exchanged a few sentences with my colleagues there, and then I went back to my post in the winery sector. That is to say that in the course of that day there was no opportunity for me to come into any contact with that area around Ovcara. In the previous days, it was customary when touring the PVO units. And I probably would have gone there on that day too, had it not been for these other duties and commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Had you visited the LAD at Ovcara before the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. I went to the command post of the commander there, commander of our artillery battalion of PVO when previously he was appointed local commander by the commander of the 80th Brigade, and I used to tour in that sector the deployment positions of various batches of the artillery battalion, in the Broda area of their area of responsibility. The regular procedure is, when touring some units, to go to the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm interested in whether you had gone there on one occasion or more than one occasion. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. It would be hard for me to tell you now off-the-cuff how many times I went there, but I went to visit them regularly during that period of time, because that was my regular duty, to tour the area, to analyse, assess the situation, and give any technical assistance as needed and solve any problems that might have come up. So that I would visit them regularly, sometimes even more than once a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how long had they been there, had that unit been there?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the Ovcara area? Or just in the area of responsibility? When we handed over our duties, they remained there, and we went back. So from the moment when the 80th Motorised Brigade took over that area from the 20th Brigade, the situation that we already described today, throughout the period, in order to expand its responsibilities from the 22nd, it covered the entire area of Vukovar. Yesterday I said that the 80th Brigade came in stages. Most likely this is how they mobilised battalions, and as battalions were mobilised, they would be deployed to that area. And this is why there was a period of time from the 8th onwards when the artillery battalion arrived until the 11th when the Guards Brigade took care of logistical support, until the 80th Brigade was developed enough in order to provide its own logistical support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And all of that is in November of 1991, is it?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Had you had reason to visit Ovcara before the 80th Motorised Brigade moved into the area?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I would pass through and as somebody who was in charge of anti-aircraft defence, there was no need for me to stay there longer. I would pass through on my way to the deployment sector of the 3rd Assault Detachment. It's either the third or the fourth one, and that was in the area of Vucedol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you had no anti-aircraft unit in that area during the time you had been there as the Guards Brigade or OGS until the 80th Motorised Brigade commenced to arrive?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the PVO artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade was the first one to arrive, out of all units of the 80th Brigade, it was deployed in that area. It was not specifically in Ovcara, but in that broader area towards Mitnica. Between Negoslavci and Ovcara, in that general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did you determine where it should be deployed when it arrived?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Based on the task that I received and after, during an assessment, I, as a specialist organ, in order to cover that entire area, had to decide on the deployment. I also had to take into account the criteria that we spoke of yesterday. We had to cover the entire area. We couldn't have any blind spots. So taking the units that we had available, I did my best to deploy them in the most efficient way, in that area. The artillery battalion of the Guards Brigade, the artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade and the one from the 211th Armoured Brigade, those who had already been there, in order to unify the forces were deployed in that area. And that was in accordance with the order that had been issued. And then I, based on it, made a proposal and I had to take into account the criteria specified in the order for the PVO, the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When had there last been an air attack by the Croatian air force?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to recall the exact date, but it was on the 10th or 11th of November. During the night, they dropped some boilers filled with explosives from some 2000 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that from helicopter or fixed wing?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was fixed wing. The weather was quite bad, visibility was low and they weren't really capable of targetting, but their reasoning was, whatever we hit will be fine. So they would just fly over, drop these boilers and then fly away. Given our weapons, they decided to fly above 2.000 metres and they also took advantage of the bad weather, and also it was night-time. So all of that worked into their favour. Fortunately, there were no casualties there. They just hit a building and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So if there had been an attack on the 10th or 11th of November, you had that in mind when you determined where the anti-aircraft battery of the 80th Brigade should be placed?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind everyone, regardless of whose artillery battalion it was or whose battery it was. I had to take into account the calibre, the equipment that artillery battalions had, and I had to take all of that into account to cover a certain area, and also in order to satisfy the requirement that the units be present in the area where there was action so that we wouldn't need to move one unit from one deployment sector to another deployment sector. Normally, that is not done unless artillery and rocket units are resubordinated. Only in that situation they are deployed, based on the plans of the commander under whom they are. And in that situation, they leave the organisational structure of their original unit and go elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that you gave all of these factors consideration when you determined where the battery should be placed?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, when did the battery move?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The batteries did not move. I mean, the firing portion of batteries, except that pursuant to a request of the commander of the 80th Brigade, the command post was relocated. It was in the sector of Sajmiste when the artillery battalion arrived. It was there because the accommodation for them was there. And I repeat that it was under the request of the commander of the 80th Brigade that this command post was relocated to Ovcara. I suppose that this was done because the commander of the 80th Brigade, upon receiving the task from the commander of OG South, did this. He proposed this, and yesterday we were able to see that this was implemented. This did not affect the organisation of the anti-aircraft defence at all. That is to say, that the firing segments were not moved, because there was no need to do that. We normally only moved them when they are uncovered and when they're exposed to the enemy fire. We move them in order to protect them, or we move them in order to group for a mass attack, or something like that. And since there was no major danger from any enemy activity from the air space, there was no need for us to move them to any additional reserve firing positions. Now, what I just told you pertains to the firing segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The command post at Ovcara, can you tell me when you first visited that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact time, but on the same day, the commander of the artillery battalion told me that he had been given an additional duty, and he wanted me to give him rules of service. Maybe he would not have informed me about this, but he needed the rules of service. He was assigned to the post of local commander and he needed to become familiar with his duties, that's why he needed the rules of service. It was his -- duty-bound to establish everything in accordance with the rules of service, and he had to ensure that the organisational structure was right, that the records were kept properly, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are not able to say what day that was?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this was on the same day when he was -- I can't remember the exact date, but it was on the same day when the commander appointed him local commander or town commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why do you say that? I understood from your evidence you didn't know that he had been. You weren't consulted beforehand, were you?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for me to be consulted. One commander suggested this to another commander, and that was resolved. It didn't affect the organisational structure of PVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, when the commander spoke to you, did he come to you? Or were you visiting the command post?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, he came to see me. He asked for the rules of service, and this is when he informed me about this. And also he needed to keep me up-to-date, that was his duty. Whenever there were any changes about the deployment of our forces, he needed to inform me, in order for me to enter that information into our map. We needed a cut-off date, and we needed to put in proper changes into the documents. So this can't be kept a secret. He can't be relocated and keep it a secret without disclosing it to me, because he needs to leave his prior post and all ties with him are cut off, and then there's an interruption, a disruption in the command and control system and in the communication system. This is why all of this needs to be- this is why there is a need to have communication between all forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of November, are you clear in your mind that you didn't visit the command post at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no possibility for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that day of events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Had you heard anything about events at Ovcara on the day before, the 19th or the day before that, the 18th?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything. Most likely, had something happened there, we would have been informed during our briefings. There were no secrets, no secrets were kept. We discussed all issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you didn't visit Ovcara on any of those days?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go prior to that, but I wouldn't be able to tell you now off-the-cuff exactly on which date. As I told you, I went to visit the units that were on their positions, and I would stop briefly, in passing, at the command post of the commander, and perhaps if he was away visiting some firing positions, then there was no need for me to stop at the command post at all. We would go to locations where our people were. We would go to firing positions of our units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know it's hard for you to remember after this time, but are you able to say how many times you went to that command post at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command post specifically? Perhaps twice. Maybe twice. And as for that general area, I would tour my units on a daily basis. You know, we had many tasks and there was not much time to do everything. And as a commander, I had to tour the entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How close to the Ovcara command post was your nearest other unit?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was to the south-west of Ovcara, 500, 600 metres, up to a kilometre, 500 to 600 metres, about there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what type of unit was that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a battery, 30/2 millimetres, and that was near the road leading to Vukovar from Negoslavci to Vukovar and then the area away from Ovcara to the south-west of Ovcara, towards Mitnica. This is where the firing position of that battery was, 30/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you normally approach that from the Negoslavci-Vukovar road.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One could reach it from that area, but in bad weather, if there's a lot of mud, one would take a different road and cut at a 90 degree angle, because it was a shortcut. But one didn't have to go to Ovcara first. There was no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to your command on the 20th of November, after having finished with the exhumation and identification mission for the day, did you hear anything then from anybody about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing. I had visited the command post, the Guards Brigade division command post where the headquarters of Operations Group South was, and that was my place, too.
