There were three active duty soldiers, one corporal, and one military conscript from the Guards Brigade. There were many questions raised by soldiers, officers from whose units these soldiers were. We spent quite some time informing them, and trying to figure out who should go to the burial on the 23rd, since a burial was planned of a soldier in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we had no other activities, because everything that was of any importance to us, who were in the anti-aircraft defence had already been concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic. Is there a transcript problem? Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 45, line 7, 8 and 9, where exactly was the witness? Can he just specify the location, because he used an acronym again and I think it has been misrecorded as a consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to help, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What acronyms are we talking about? Because I didn't -- Mr. Vasic can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked him, Your Honours, where he went after the exhumation and that was the question, and the answer was misrecorded, that's all.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the exhumation I went to, to where my place was in the Sajmiste area, because that's where the VOJ air surveillance and reporting headquarters was for Operations Group South, and at the same time the observation post in the winery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what I had understood you to say, but Mr. Vasic is now happy. Yes. While you were there, did you hear from any of your battery commanders?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, you mean when I got back from the briefing? Is that what you have in mind? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have in mind --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That period of time? That time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Precisely when you arrived, after dealing with the exhumations and the identifications, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, on the phone, since I couldn't for a short time, I phoned all the units, I first asked the duty operations officers at the centre to ask them if there was anything new, according to the record that morning, but nothing of any consequence to the PVO or to any of our organisational units, at least that's what the report indicated. I spoke to the commanders, and I spoke to the PVO division commander of the Guards Brigade in person because he remained there. I prepared for the briefing and I was on my way to the commander for the five o'clock briefing. I did not go anywhere else to visit or see anyone on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you say you spoke to the commanders, how many people is that? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, primarily the commander of the Guards Brigade, the commander of the Guards Brigade division, and the commander of the 80th Brigade division. I did not get any information from them that would be of any consequence, of any particular consequence in the sense of there being a need to step in and do something or in the sense of needing to go and speak to the commander of OG South. It was nothing much. It was that simple. The situation was slowly getting back to normal and we were already thinking about our return. And those commitments that unfortunately we still had, such as burying the mortal remains of those members of the Guards Brigade who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you spoke to only two commanders? Or were there more?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no need to speak to anyone else, because there was nothing much happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You don't need to explain everything when a question is asked, yes. Now the commander of the -- from the Guards Brigade to whom you spoke, his name?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain First Class Stanko Mijatovic. That was the rank he had at the time; now he's a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade, Marcek. Jon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you did that by telephone or were you in a position to speak to either of those people personally?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Face-to-face I spoke to the artillery battery commander, Captain Mijatovic, the artillery battery of the Guards Brigade, because he was there. The artillery battalion. And if he hadn't been there, we would have had to meet anyway because I was just back from a less than pleasant mission, and all three of those men were members of his unit. Up to this point in time he had known nothing about those men, and they were still recorded as missing at the time. We knew nothing of their fate. That was his number 1 assignment, clearing the terrain, setting up teams, burials, monitoring, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the other commander from the 80th Motorised Brigade, did you speak to him face-to-face, or not?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Anything new? Nothing much. Fine. That's it. Anything important to do with the assignments of our branch? He would have dealt with all the other issues with his own commander. Why would I need to look into that, something that was of no consequence to me? If there was anything to be raised, he should have raised it with the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're speaking about "would have" and "should have." Do you have a clear recollection today of that particular afternoon?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th? The 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. A clear recollection. I set out in the morning, I took the pathologist, Stankovic, there. The investigators were there. The civilians who had been captured by the Ustashas in a building across the way indicated the exact location. And that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you hold. You are starting off on another of your long explanations.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hold, please. Thank you. In particular are you able to remember clearly everyone that you met that day?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be quite a long list were I to remember every single person that I met on that day. The reason being everybody wanted -- I mean this is new information. These three soldiers, we knew nothing about those three soldiers up to this point in time. They had been treated as missing persons. I was on the spot. I was watching the whole thing. I was of interest to everyone for purely information purposes unfortunately. Therefore, I could hardly give you a list of men and officers at the time that I spoke to, because there were so many questions to be raised, questions to be raised by individuals in relation to all those unpleasant developments and events, dead bodies, burned bodies. The pathologist, Mr. Stankovic took quite some time and had to apply a lengthy procedure before he was finally able to identify the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What reminded you that it was on the 20th that you had to undertake this exhumation and identification procedure? Did you have a record of that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, because of this unpleasant atmosphere. I got this special assignment and that was the first time I met Stankovic, the pathologist. And being there that morning, that's what is lodged in my memory. An especially in view of the fact that this was the very first time that I had witnessed anything like that, extremely unpleasant, but being a soldier, well it was something I just had to cope with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can well imagine. It would not be easy. But why do you feel confident that that was on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply remember that day. As for any link up, that was the day before what, two or three days, because we were planning to leave and this was done immediately when access was granted and when we were told we were now able to access the scene and do what we had to do. And until such time as we were told where the exact location was where this needed to be done, there was nothing we could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would it affect what you've been saying if it were the case that the LAD unit of the 80th Brigade moved its command post on the 18th of November to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I fully understand the question but -- well, here's the answer. It would have had no effect whatsoever, this is when we received this information when the pathologist and the investigators were due to arrive, so that we could have the regular kind of procedure applied on the spot which had nothing to do with any moves or anything. And this is at the opposite Ovcara, it's to the east of Vukovar and this is exactly at the opposite end. It was a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a different area, I think it was assault detachment number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. You have been telling us, though, that you had visited the command post of Ovcara after it moved there and you've told us that you didn't go to Ovcara on the 18th or the 19th or the 20th. Well, if the command post didn't move there until the 18th, does that mean that there is something faulty in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did say that I did pass by once, briefly, as I was on my way through. I can't remember the exact date. I was on my way to Vucedol, and in order to get there you need to cross Ovcara. So it wasn't like I was on my way to see the commander specifically to visit him. Rather, he comes from the same branch as I do and I just dropped in on him, spent several minutes there, no more, and was again on my way to Vucedol, I had a special mission there, which I had received from the commander to do with visiting an element of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've also had evidence that you and the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade LAD spoke at about 4 o'clock on the 20th at your command post on the 20th of November. Could that have happened? I understand that you were under great pressure with your dead soldiers, from what you say.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly tell you whether that was -- but it was at the same time, when I was back from the brief, briefing the time could have been around 16 -- could have been. 15. I know we finished. I know exactly. And then I went back. I had lunch. I heard from him. It could be, it could be around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you heard from him on the phone or speaking to him personally? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the phone, only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's your recollection of the 20th that he didn't visit you personally at your command post?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you went straight from your command post to the briefing at OG South?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Negoslavci, yes. Yes. Straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Weiner, is there anything arising from that, that you would like to explore?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you visit Ovcara, the Ovcara command post after November 20th?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 20th of November, no. I did not. I had other special missions and on the 23rd I spent the whole day leading a team to Novi Sad I took them there to attend a burial and we spent the entire day there. We had a lot of things to do. We had to prepare a lot of things. We had to return some extra equipment and everything, that we had on our minds at the time, and then we had to prepare our return. In the meantime, they had taken over, so as far as PVO was concerned, there was no need for me to get in touch with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What time did you return on the 23rd, if you spent the whole day in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right, right. The burial took place in the evening. It was nearly dark. We stayed there. We visited the family. It was late. It could have been past ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you testify today that you were present when Colonel Marcek wrote that report to the 1st Military District, Mrksic? Didn't you testify to that today?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, nor did I ever say that. I think you were the one who said it. We can look at the transcript and see. See if you can find a spot where I am actually saying that. He couldn't possibly have written to the 1st Military District because he has his own commander and this is something that his commander should write. The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 426, which we showed you today, Colonel Mrksic, that command report. Were you there?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please point that out to me? Please, bring it up. There's too much information for me to remember every single bit. Can you please show me what Marcek wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You just testified you weren't home until very late on the 23rd. Today you testified: "I know this because I was present when it was agreed to send this particular report, because as far as I can remember, on the very next day the commander of the 80th Brigade wrote reports." Were you present, sir, on the 23rd, or were you in Novi Sad on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd I was in Novi Sad. I commented on what was shown and I answered questions in relation to the document that was shown. I never, for a moment, stated it was about my memory. My memory was very specific. You asked me to comment on that report. How the OG South commander could write this on the 23rd, whereas all the commitments had been handed over on the 22nd? It was these circumstances that I was commenting on in answering you about. I never said I was there when this was written. You asked me a specific question. I gave you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you speak with the LAD PVO commander of the 80th on the 21st, the 22nd, or the 23rd of November?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As soon as on the 19th, so that was earlier, from the 19th on the tasks and obligations, in terms of PVO, were secondary. There was no need for me, in addition to all of my other commitments, to see him. I knew that already on the 22nd the brigade would be taking over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you speak to him on the 21st, 22nd or 23rd?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20, the 22nd, the 23rd, I can't remember, the 20 -- the 21st, I can't remember for that matter. There was no special need in terms of PVO for us to do anything at all. And there was so many other special missions and so many things that needed doing, regarding our return. You know, when you have a preparation stage and then you have these three dead bodies to deal with, and all your usual daily business on top of everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that plans were -- that plans were made on the 22nd to move the command post of the LAD PVO of the 80th out of Ovcara, and it did in fact move on the 23rd. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And final question. Do you know when Mr. Stankovic arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly when he arrived. I know when I met him and that when we were off to the scene, that was in the morning hours and my assumption is he had arrived earlier that same morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Now, Mr. Vasic I asked you to wait earlier, because I was confident we were going to come to you and we want to get this part over fairly quickly. Is there anything you would like to ask either out of what I asked the witness or Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The problem was a matter of the interpretation and the monitor said something else, because the interpretation was Marcek and the monitor said Mrksic, I think that might have misled the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, my learned friend told you that you had previously stated that you had been there for the writing of this report. Were you there when the report was written, or were you there when the handover took place? The one that occurred on the 22nd of November, between OG South and the 80th Motorised Brigade, that handover.

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the handover took place, but I was at the command when we put the finishing touches to our files, to our documents, when we discussed what we should leave behind, when we discussed whether our records should be drawn up, and when we sorted out all of these papers. And they, both commanders, got their assignments once the assignment had been over. There was no need for any guidance. They just went back to their own places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend, you said that on that day you saw for the first time Mr. Stankovic. Was that also the first time you learned that he was in the area of Vukovar on that day, the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: Milovan Lesanovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the previous day, I was given an assignment by the commander. He told me that we had received information about the location of these three corpses, we were told in whose yard they were, and I was given an assignment to go and meet an investigative judge and the pathologist and to go with them to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. You will be pleased to know that completes the questions for you. We would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance you've given, and you are now free to return to your ordinary activities. And the Court officer will show you out. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to give you my best regards, to thank you for your patience. I hope that my evidence will assist you in your work, and that it would facilitate your assessing the entire situation and establishing the truth. I would also like to greet my three colleagues. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there is no other witness today. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, our next witness will arrive this weekend and will be ready to come into the Court room on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some submissions which we hope to be able to hear now. I think for everybody -- Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning the submissions, we had two submissions planned for today. One was Hadzic and one was the statements. Yesterday we spoke with Mr. Lukic, and we had agreed that it would be in the best interests to have Defence file their submissions in relation to the statements on Monday. It's going to be all new submissions. We will not be able to respond to them because it's new matters. And they had agreed to file them in writing on Monday, which we had no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you want us not to hear submissions now, to allow written submissions to be filed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- for you to consider them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And hopefully we may be able to reach them perhaps on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Weiner, yes..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we're not too busy, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We could however argue the Hadzic issue if you want which is the video, the admissibility of that videotape which has been before the Court, or we could wait for Tuesday or Monday for all of the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will hear all of the submissions at the one time, I think, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so, we will now adjourn until Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of September, 2006 at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.05 p.m.,
